newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Brazil expects ATPC survival, sees free tin market.
newsitem.headline: Brazil expects ATPC survival, sees free tin market.

text.p: The head of the Brazilian delegation to the Association of Tin Producing Countries (ATPC) said on Thursday he expected the organisation to hold together, despite the withdrawal of Thailand and Australia as members.

"We expect so (the ATPC to continue). Even if there are only five countries, they still together account for 85 percent of world production," Miguel Navarrede-Fernandez, general director of Brazil's Ministry of Mines and Energy, told reporters.
He was attending an ATPC council meeting in Singapore prior to a full ministerial meeting to be held on Monday and Tuesday.
Indonesia, Malaysia, Bolivia, China and Nigeria remain members of the ATPC. Zaire also belongs, but now produces almost no tin and has stopped attending meetings. Brazil has observer status.
Thailand has said it would withdraw from October 1 and Australia has announced it will pull out on December 10.
"They are leaving because their production is deceasing and they are to become net importers," Navarrede-Fernandez said.

He added that the ATPC proposed to maintain the de facto free market in tin, as its export quota scheme has been widely ignored by producers, for a year and then would decide whether to replace the quotas with a new scheme at its next ministerial meeting.
Navarrede-Fernandez estimated world stocks of tin would be around 36,000 tonnes at the end of this year, compared with about 30,000 tonnes on December 31, 1995.
He attributed the forecast rise in inventories to an increase in tin production in Indonesia.
